blocks.text: Laura lowered herself against the ventilator and put her hands in her lap.

The metal was cold through her coat. From this height, the brass funnel seemed to occupy most of the space in front of her. Daniel had left the machine where they had tested it. Its wheels still rested against the timber chocks.
He took the rope from the top of the vent.
“In front,” she said, holding out her wrists.
Daniel glanced at her hands, then at the place where a visitor would come down to face her.
“Yes. Let him see them.”

He passed the rope around the housing and brought it across her middle. Laura lifted her elbows while he worked, then lowered them when he asked. The turns held her upper arms against her sides, with her forearms resting across her lap.
She watched him wind the remaining length around her wrists. A short span joined the binding at her hands to the rope across her coat. He drew it firm and finished the knot beside her hip.
Laura pulled her hands apart.
The rope held.
“That'll do.”
Daniel sat back on his heels and examined the result. Laura looked past him into the brass mouth, her boots planted on the gravel between it and the vent.
blocks.alt: Daniel finishes the ordinary rope holding fully costumed Laura against the low rooftop vent while bodyless Luke watches from beside the idle collector.

blocks.text: Luke drifted nearer. His eyes followed the rope around the metal housing.
“Can she get loose?”
Laura looked up at him.
“I'm sitting right here.”
Daniel checked the knot once more. “She only has to stay there until he comes.”
He stood and went to the stairhouse. When he returned, he carried a folded piece of gray canvas.

Laura shifted her shoulders. The rope moved with her coat, but the turns around the vent kept her from leaning forward. She settled back, irritated by how quickly sitting still had become uncomfortable.

Daniel spread the canvas over the collector's cylinder and tucked it around the far end. The cloth broke up the shape of the glass and coils. From the parapet, it might have been another piece of machinery waiting for someone to finish repairing it.
He left the brass mouth uncovered. On the western side, a lifted fold gave him access to the meters and switches.
Luke watched him lower himself behind the trolley.
The canvas stopped moving. Daniel's white coat disappeared below the rail.
Laura could still see the toes of his shoes.
“A little farther back.”
He drew them in.

Luke moved into the clear strip beside the western controls. From there he could watch the northern end of the roof through the space beside the vent. The taller warehouse wall stood behind him, its bricked-up window losing the last light.
The cable lay where they had put it, close to the wall before turning toward the machine. Nothing crossed the open gravel in front of Laura.
She turned her wrists together. The rope dragged across the seam of one glove.
“Ready,” Daniel said from behind the canvas.
Laura looked above the parapet.

For a moment, she could think only of how foolish she would look if nothing happened. Daniel was crouched behind his machine. Luke had stopped arguing. Both of them were waiting for something she had never tried to do on purpose.
She opened her mouth.
“I need help.”
The words went out over the roof. A truck changed gear in the street below.
Laura waited, watching a scrap of cloud drift between two buildings. The sky stayed empty.
She had heard Flaming Head clearly beside the lake. She remembered looking at his mouth, certain that somebody else must be speaking. He had come because he had felt that she needed him.
Now she was thinking about Daniel's shoes and the rope on her wrists.
She let her head rest against the vent.
Below the roof, a door slammed. It brought back the apartment for an instant: standing inside after her boyfriend had gone, still holding the door as though he might come back for something.
Then the water, and the terrible waiting afterward.
She held on to how it had felt to want an answer. Under everything she intended to do here, that part was easy to find.
“I just need somebody to help me,” Laura said. “Please.”
blocks.alt: Laura sits with her gloved wrists bound in her lap, her face and mouth clear, looking toward the twilight sky as she deliberately asks Flaming Head for help.

blocks.text: Her hands had tightened without her noticing. She loosened them and looked toward the sky again.
This time she kept looking.
Flaming Head turned above the shoreline rocks.
A wave struck below him and broke into pale spray. Farther out, a boat was moving toward the harbor, its lights beginning to show against the dark water.
He had been watching it when the feeling reached him.
Someone needed help.
He moved nearer the path. Two people were walking there, one carrying a folded newspaper. Neither looked up. A cyclist passed them and continued along the shore.
The feeling drew him inland.
He rose above the trees. The path and its walkers fell away beneath him. Beyond the roofs, windows were taking on the first lights of evening.
Something in that need was familiar.

He remembered Laura beside the water, keeping her distance while she tried to explain what happened whenever she spat. Later she had stood in the costume he had made and watched him as though every answer he gave made things worse.
She had wanted him to understand. At their last meeting, she had wanted him gone.
The feeling came again.
Flaming Head left the water behind and flew toward the lower industrial roofs.
blocks.alt: A bright, healthy Flaming Head turns away from Lake Erie and flies inland toward the familiar sense that someone needs him.

blocks.text: He crossed a street above a bus turning at the corner. For a little way the buildings hid the direction from him. He slowed above an intersection, letting the familiar need draw him onward, then turned toward a taller stretch of brickwork.
The last of the sunlight lay across its upper windows. Below them, a lower roof was already in shadow.
A movement caught his eye near its northern edge.
He went higher.
Laura heard gravel shift beside the collector.
Luke had risen far enough to look past the vent. His eyes were fixed above the parapet.
“There.”
Daniel's hand appeared beneath the lifted fold of canvas. He pointed once toward the roof, and Luke dropped out of sight beside the control box.
Laura looked where Luke had been looking.
A small orange light moved above the neighboring roof.
She drew a breath through her nose. Her wrists pressed together. The thing she had imagined while Daniel marked the workshop floor was crossing the sky toward her.
The light stopped.
For a moment she thought he had seen enough and would go away.
“Please,” she said again, more quietly.
She saw him turn.
From above the parapet, Flaming Head could see the top of the ventilator and Laura's hair against it.
He moved around the housing until her face came into view.
She was sitting on the roof. Rope passed around her coat and disappeared behind the metal box. Her gloved hands lay together in her lap, bound too.
He stopped above her.
Behind him stood a trolley beneath a gray sheet. Its brass funnel pointed toward the place where he would have to come down. A heavy cable ran away from it toward the taller brick wall.
He moved slightly to one side. The funnel caught his light.
Laura tried to lift her hands. The rope drew tight across her coat and stopped them.
He looked back at her face.
Whatever had happened between them beside the lake, she was tied here now. Leaving her would mean leaving her with whoever had done it.
Flaming Head came lower, until Laura could see the concern in his eyes instead of only the brightness of the flame.
blocks.alt: Flaming Head arrives beside bound Laura on the established rooftop; the collector waits beneath gray canvas with its brass intake open, still switched off.

blocks.text: “Laura?”
The voice reached her as clearly as it had beside the water. His mouth had not moved.
For a moment, her answer caught in her throat.
Behind him, the canvas hung still over the collector. There was no hum.
Laura looked into the little face that had come when she asked.
“Help me,” she said.
